transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. What brings you into the clinic today?

Hi. Well, the main reason I’m here is that I'm having a really hard time at work. I'm a nurse, and on the floor, I just... I lose my train of thought constantly. An IV pump will beep, or someone asks another nurse a question, or a call light goes off, and suddenly I’ve completely forgotten what patient flow issue I was even working on. It's just happening all the time.
How long have you been dealing with this difficulty with staying focused and getting easily distracted?
Well, it's been a major problem since I took on the expanded charge-nurse responsibilities. That was... almost two years ago. It's just been really tough since then.
Did you experience similar difficulties with attention or staying focused while growing up, such as during elementary or high school?

Yeah, I did. Um, even back in elementary school, my teachers would always write on my report cards that I was bright, but careless. I was always losing my worksheets or just completely forgetting to turn my homework in. My mom actually had to sit with me every single night just to keep me on track and make sure I actually finished it.
Outside of work, do you find yourself dealing with constant, uncontrollable worry about a variety of everyday things?

No, not really. I mean, I definitely get stressed about work because of how much I'm struggling to keep up there, but... no, I don't just sit around worrying about everyday things. Outside of work, I wouldn't say I'm an anxious person at all. It's really just the focus and losing track of things that's getting to me.
Have you been experiencing persistent feelings of sadness, feeling down, or feeling hopeless?

No, I wouldn't say that. I get frustrated with myself, especially when I mess up at work or forget something important, but I don't feel depressed or hopeless. It's really just the frustration of not being able to keep my head on straight.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits chronic, pervasive symptoms of inattention and high distractibility by external stimuli leading to significant occupational impairment. History confirms childhood onset (elementary school difficulties, losing worksheets, forgetting homework, requiring parental supervision) and persistence into adulthood lasting well over 6 months, fulfilling criteria for ADHD (predominantly inattentive presentation).
